evidence.title: Impact of Commercial Artificial Intelligence on Radiologist Reading Time for Pulmonary Nodule Evaluation at Chest CT
evidence.outcome: Operational metric (reporting time) and projected workforce and financial impact after AI deployment
evidence.effect: Median reporting time decreased 21.3 to 18.2 minutes (14.6%); exploratory modeling suggested about 0.5 FTE radiologist workload reduction at institutional volumes.
evidence.quote: At institutional scan volumes (approximately 20 000-22 000 chest CT examinations annually), exploratory modeling suggested an approximate reduction of 0.5 full-time equivalent radiologist workload.

evidence.title: Analgesia quality index improves the quality of postoperative pain management: a retrospective observational study of 14,747 patients between 2014 and 2021
evidence.outcome: Moderate-to-severe postoperative pain and adverse reactions with AQI-guided performance monitoring
evidence.effect: Control versus AQI: pain 26.3% vs. 21.7%; ratio difference -4.6% (95% CI, -6% to -3.2%; P < 0.001). Total adverse events: 18.1% vs. 19.2%; P = 0.09.
evidence.quote: The incidence of moderate-to-severe pain was 26.3% in the control group and 21.7% in the experimental group.

evidence.title: The BestShape artificial intelligence system for real-time prediction of intradialytic hypotension-clinical outcomes after four-year follow-up
evidence.outcome: Clinical, financial, and satisfaction KPIs tracked after AI deployment
evidence.effect: Reductions in IDH, CPR, and falls; estimated annual cost savings USD 115,658; mean personnel satisfaction score 86.
evidence.quote: The estimated annual cost savings by implementing BestShape were USD 115 658.

commentary.bottom_line: Three before-and-after studies in which health systems tracked defined metrics after deploying an AI tool reported gains in reporting time, postoperative pain, dialysis complications, and cost, but none compared KPI tracking against no tracking. The evidence suggests that outcome-linked KPIs can be measured in real deployments, while whether defining them prevents low-value tools from persisting remains untested.

perspectives.view: One quasi-experimental study and two pre-post studies without comparators report favorable results. Observational designs start at low certainty, and certainty drops further because each study tests an AI tool with metrics attached rather than the practice of KPI tracking itself. No study reports whether tracking led a system to modify or retire a tool.

In 14,747 surgical patients, moderate-to-severe pain fell from 26.3% to 21.7% under AI-guided performance monitoring, while total adverse events changed from 18.1% to 19.2% (P = 0.09). Tracking a safety metric next to the target metric allowed that possible signal to be seen. The dialysis study reported fewer falls and CPR events, although it did not give rates.

The dialysis program tracked clinical, financial, and staff-satisfaction measures across 213,071 sessions, which suggests that measuring several domains at once may be workable in routine operations. None of the three studies reports the staff time, data infrastructure, or analytic effort needed to maintain the metrics over time.

Median chest CT reporting time fell from 21.3 to 18.2 minutes, and exploratory modeling projected about 0.5 FTE of radiologist workload reduction. The dialysis program estimated USD 115,658 in annual savings. These figures show that financial and workforce effects can be estimated, but the estimates are modeled, not audited, and they omit the cost of the monitoring.

The studies took place in China, Taiwan, and one setting the authors did not report. None stratified KPIs by payer, language, or literacy, so the data cannot show whether aggregate gains extended to disadvantaged patients or hid differences between groups.

commentary.research_gap: No study compares health systems or tools with outcome-linked KPI programs against those without them. Such a study would need to measure whether tracking leads to earlier detection of tools that underperform, to decommissioning decisions, or to recovery of hidden costs. Studies should also report what it costs to run the monitoring and should present KPIs by patient subgroup.
commentary.underserved_note: No test reported enrolling or stratifying Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, and one study did not report its setting. Health systems serving these patients cannot assume that the reported benefits apply to them and may need to break their own KPIs down by these groups to find out.
